This is probably the best small-catchment test bed in the US for a HEC-RAS 2D rain-on-grid model.

**Why it works:**
- **DEM:** Maryland has statewide QL1/QL2 lidar. Howard County 1 m (and in places 0.5 ft-accuracy) bare-earth DEM is on The National Map and OpenTopography.
- **Rainfall:** Two well-documented catastrophic flash floods ?€? 30 July 2016 and 27 May 2018 ?€? both with radar and gauge coverage, plus NOAA Atlas 14 Vol. 2 design storms for the site.
- **Size:** The Tiber Branch/Hudson Branch catchment is only about 4?€?7 sq mi. A 3?€?5 m mesh runs on a laptop in minutes, so you can actually iterate on mesh, Manning's *n*, and infiltration.
- **Literature:** Both events have been modeled repeatedly in published papers, so you have something to benchmark against.

**Watch out for:** the lower reach through Main Street runs through a large conduit/culvert system. You'll either need to represent it as an SA/2D connection or accept that the surface-only model over-predicts street flow. Also note there is no long-record USGS gauge on Tiber Branch itself ?€? gauging there is post-2018 ?€? so calibration leans on high-water marks from the USGS Short-Term Network flood event viewer rather than a hydrograph.

**Brays Bayou or Halls Bayou, Harris County, Texas.** Harris County Flood Control District operates 201 gauge stations measuring rainfall and stream stage, and its Flood Warning System site serves data for more than 350 stations across the region including partner agencies ?€? 15-minute data, free, going back decades. 1 m lidar via TxGIO. ## Route A ?€? the OpenTopography portal (needs qualifying access)

1. Click **Sign In** at the top right of that page and create/log into an account. If you don't have a .edu address, apply through opentopography.org/content/how-access-restricted-data-opentopography, or use OT+.

The same OpenTopography page links to this: `https://prd-tnm.s3.amazonaws.com/index.html?prefix=StagedProducts/Elevation/1m/`. But the friendlier front end is The National Map:

chat:
Split this into three groups: is the solver healthy, is the physics plausible, and does it agree with anything independent. Run them in that order ?€? no point assessing physics if the numerics are broken.

## 1. Numerical health

Check these in the computation log before you look at a single map.

| Metric | Where | Pass criterion |
|---|---|---|
| Volume accounting error | Computation log, end of run | < 1%. Above 2% means the run is unusable |
| Courant number | Log, per timestep | Staying at or below 1.0 |
| Adaptive timestep halving | Log | Occasional is fine; constant halving means bad cells |
| Iterations to convergence | Log | Hitting the 20 max repeatedly means non-convergence |
| Cells with WSE errors | Log warnings | Should be zero or a handful, all at the mesh edge |
| Runtime | Log | Sanity check against expectation |

## 2. Mass balance ?€? your strongest check

With infiltration off, this is exact arithmetic and it's the single most diagnostic number you have.

Rainfall input: 0.0257 m ?? 26.63 km?? = **~684,000 m??**

Total outflow volume through the Normal Depth boundary, plus water still stored on the grid at the end of the run, should sum to that. Get outflow by integrating the outlet hydrograph. If they don't match, you have a leak ?€? usually water escaping across an unbounded mesh edge, or a BC line that doesn't span the full valley.

Derived from the same: **runoff coefficient** should be 1.0. Anything less means water left the domain somewhere it shouldn't.

## 3. Physical plausibility

| Metric | Expected here | Red flag |
|---|---|---|
| Peak discharge at outlet | ~8?€?15 m??/s | Orders of magnitude off |
| Time to peak | 2?€?3 hr after rain starts (Tc ??? 3 hr) | Peak during the 10-min storm |
| Recession shape | Smooth decay over hours | Sawtooth or steps |
| Channel velocity | 0.5?€?2 m/s | > 5 m/s sustained |
| Overland velocity | 0.05?€?0.5 m/s | > 1 m/s on hillslopes |
| Channel depth | 0.3?€?1.5 m | > 3 m in a first-order valley |
| Hillslope depth | mm to a few cm | > 0.1 m on ridgetops |
| Froude number | < 1 nearly everywhere | Widespread supercritical flow |

**Flow path check.** Overlay the maximum depth raster on NHD flowlines for the area. Your wet cells should trace the mapped drainage network. Where they don't ?€? water pooling in a field, a channel that goes dry mid-reach ?€? you've found a mesh face cutting across a valley, and that's a breakline problem.

**Ponding check.** Persistent standing water in places with no depression in the terrain means the mesh isn't conveying properly.

## 4. Independent benchmarks

Since you have no gauge in this catchment, these are how you get an external reality check.

- **USGS StreamStats** (streamstats.usgs.gov) ?€? delineate the same catchment, and it returns regional regression peak-flow quantiles for ungauged Iowa basins. Compare your modelled peak against the 10-year estimate. Same order of magnitude is a pass; this is the closest thing to validation you'll get here.
- **NHD channel network** ?€? geometric check on flow paths, as above.
- **Iowa Flood Center inundation maps** ?€? where they exist nearby, a qualitative extent comparison.

## 5. Sensitivity and convergence

Worth running once you have a working baseline. Change one thing at a time and see whether the answer moves.

- **Mesh convergence**: rerun at 20 m and 10 m. If peak flow shifts more than ~10% between 15 m and 10 m, your mesh is too coarse.
- **Manning's n**: try 0.04 and 0.08. Peak timing should shift noticeably, peak magnitude less so.
- **Equation set**: rerun with SWE. Large divergence from Diffusion Wave means momentum matters here and DW is inappropriate.
- **Timestep**: halve to 5 s. If results change, you weren't converged in time.

## What you can't claim

Without a stream gauge, high water marks, or observed inundation, there is no calibration or validation ?€? only verification that the model behaves sensibly. NSE, RMSE, percent bias, Fit Statistic and similar goodness-of-fit measures all require observations you don't have. Report this as a sensitivity and plausibility assessment, not a validated model. That's an honest and perfectly publishable framing for a methods test.
